title: Chunking and Context Limits
english: My project is about how we split documents before using them in a question answering system. The system searches for useful text and gives that text to a language model. I compared three ways of splitting it: fixed size, overlap and semantic chunking. Overlap gave the best retrieval result in this experiment. The much lower semantic answer score led to another question: how much of the text was actually reaching the models? I will show the setup, the main numbers and the length problem. The final article brings together the experiments from my earlier assignments.

title: Research Question
english: Imagine a book that is too large to put on a reader's desk. We cut it into cards, find the useful cards and give a few to the reader. That is roughly what this pipeline does. If a cut separates an answer from its explanation, the reader may miss something important. My question was whether the three cutting methods change retrieval and answer quality. Each method was tested on the same 500 questions with the same models. After seeing problems with long semantic chunks, I also checked what happened when the context was made shorter.

title: Related Research
english: Previous studies gave me reasons to compare these methods rather than assume semantic chunking would win. Qu and colleagues found that semantic chunking did not consistently help across their tasks. Kiss and colleagues reported improvements with another method called Max-Min. These results can both be valid because the algorithms and evaluations differ. My experiment uses a percentile splitter and small local models. What I add is a close look at the input limits and saved outputs in that setup. I am not introducing a new splitting algorithm or claiming to repeat those papers' full experiments.

title: Data and Pipeline
english: I used the SQuAD development dataset, which contains questions about Wikipedia articles. All 48 articles form the search collection. A shuffle with seed 42 selects 500 questions, and every method gets those same question IDs. MiniLM turns the text into vectors, and FAISS searches them. The system retrieves five chunks, but sends only the first three to FLAN-T5-base. This difference matters when we read the scores. The generator accepts at most 512 input tokens and produces up to 32 new tokens, with sampling disabled. A retrieval hit means an answer string appears in a chunk from the correct article.

title: Three Chunking Methods
english: Fixed chunking takes up to 500 characters at a time. Overlap uses the same size but repeats 50 characters around a boundary. Semantic chunking looks for large changes between sentence embeddings, using the 95th percentile as its split threshold. That number is a rule for choosing boundaries, not a measure of answer accuracy. The table shows the main practical difference. Fixed and overlap produce more than three thousand chunks averaging about five hundred characters. Semantic produces only 589, averaging 2,720 characters. Those much longer chunks are important because the models still have the same small input windows.

title: Main Results
english: The green bars show retrieval. Overlap reaches 81.8 percent, or 409 questions out of 500. Fixed reaches 75.2 percent and semantic 66.4 percent. The answer scores tell a different story. Exact Match is 58 percent for overlap, 54.8 for fixed and just 1.4 for semantic. F1 gives partial credit when some answer words match, so its scores are higher here. The semantic retriever can find chunks containing an answer, yet the generator usually fails to return it. This is why I evaluate retrieval and generation separately. Finding the text does not guarantee that the generator can use it.

title: Statistical Comparison
english: The comparison is paired because the methods answer the same questions. Overlap finds an answer where fixed fails on 58 questions. Fixed wins alone on 25. That is 33 additional hits out of 500, a gain of 6.6 percentage points. The paired interval is 3 to 10 points. McNemar tests these binary disagreements, and Holm corrects for the three comparisons within the metric. The adjusted p value is about 0.0008. For Exact Match, the interval includes zero and p is 0.1332. So I can support a retrieval gain, but I cannot confidently claim an Exact Match gain from these data.

title: Where Text Gets Lost
english: There are two places where long text can be lost. MiniLM has 256 token positions, about 254 of them available for ordinary text. An answer later in a long chunk may never affect its embedding. The generator then gets three chunks followed by the question, within a 512-token limit. Long context can push useful text or the question beyond that limit. In the semantic run, 478 of the 500 prompts were truncated. Of those, one still gave an exact answer. That leaves 477 truncated failures in the error table. The flags locate a problem, although they do not prove the cause of every wrong answer.

title: Shorter Context Check
english: To investigate this, I checked a run that kept only the first 1,500 characters of context before building the prompt. The fair comparison uses the same 300 questions before and after this change. Semantic goes from four exact answers to 74: 1.33 percent to 24.67 percent. The gain is 23.33 percentage points, with an interval from 18.33 to 28.33. Overlap stays the same and fixed drops by one point. This check was added after noticing the problem, so it is exploratory. It also changes how much evidence remains and whether the question fits. It cannot isolate the effect of semantic boundaries alone.

title: Limitations
english: The main limitation is that semantic chunking changes both the boundaries and the length of the chunks. The poor score could reflect how those long chunks interact with this pipeline. I cannot conclude that every semantic method is worse. There is also only one English dataset and one model pair. Exact Match may reject valid wording, and short answer strings can appear in irrelevant text. Questions from one article are related, which can make question bootstrap intervals too narrow. A next experiment should set token limits in advance, keep the question in the prompt and test new questions with other models.

title: Rechecking the Results
english: The repository saves predictions and scores for every question, and the analysis checks question IDs before comparing methods. My classmate Bekzhan ran run_experiment.py on his laptop, using ChatGPT to help with the commands. The saved comparison shows that all 1,500 predictions and numeric outcomes matched, with a runtime of about 65 minutes. The old machine metadata labels the operator as Codex on my computer, so the repository includes my correction and preserves the original logs. This used an existing environment, not a fresh model installation. A separate clean installation check covered the analysis. I can regenerate the Results tables and figures without running the models again.

title: Conclusion
english: The answer to my research question depends on the setup. Overlap improved retrieval here, while its Exact Match advantage remains uncertain. The original hypothesis that semantic would improve both scores was not supported. The additional check points to a useful lesson: chunk boundaries have to be considered together with model input limits. For the journal part, I selected Discover Computing because it publishes work on semantic chunking and RAG evaluation. Discover Artificial Intelligence is the backup. Their indexing records and guidelines are documented in the appendix. No journal submission or acceptance is claimed. I can also show how a reported number is calculated from the saved question rows.
